articles.title_orig: Experts worry about Nvidia’s AI chip sales in China and influence over Trump
articles.title_zh: Experts worry about Nvidia’s AI chip sales in China and influence over Trump
articles.content_orig:
On its face, the recent summit between Donald Trump and China’s president Xi Jinping didn’t change much in the world of AI regulation. Export controls were not discussed, with neither country seemingly interested in making concessions. An already tenuous trade truce was temporarily extended for just two months, and looming US controls that could drop soon could easily end that and trigger China to retaliate by cutting off exports of rare earths, analysts expect.
However, in the background of these shaky talks, Nvidia appeared to notch a big win, as China is currently mulling relaxing controls and allowing some of its biggest AI firms to import perhaps millions more of Nvidia’s banned chips over the next year.
Sources familiar with China’s talks told The Information that China’s tech oversight arm, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, asked Alibaba and ByteDance to share plans to buy Nvidia’s RTX Pro 5500 chips. Although these are gaming chips, China asked firms to detail how they plan to use them, with expectations that chips could be put into servers to help power the country’s most in-demand AI models.
Increasingly, Trump looks to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang for advice on AI, but not everybody agrees that what’s good for Nvidia is good for the United States.
Already the world’s most valuable company, Nvidia would obviously profit enormously in a world where risks are downplayed, and both countries’ priorities remain powering rapid developments in frontier AI without pumping the brakes. Some critics worry that Nvidia’s profit motivations may be steering Trump’s thinking at a pivotal moment when it may matter how well a president actually understands the risks of a new technology.
For Nvidia, a big goal since Trump took office was to open up more of China’s market so that Nvidia could start selling chips that were restricted during Joe Biden’s administration. Huang has blamed US export controls for cutting Nvidia’s share of China’s advanced AI chip market from about 95 percent to zero, The Information reported .
Trump was not an instant ally. Instead, he came into office asking “What the hell is Nvidia?” and rather than loosening Biden’s export controls, he initially tightened them further, most notably by banning exports of H200 chips to China. Trump was even thinking about breaking Nvidia up, expecting that stoking more competition among chipmakers domestically was crucial to America winning the so-called “AI race” with China .
But then he met Huang over dinner at Mar-a-Lago, where Trump said he “learned the facts of life” and understood that Nvidia as a firm is an “amazing” AI leader. Ignoring warnings from lawmakers and national security experts, Trump lifted the export controls on H200 chips , which China eventually allowed to be sold to some firms. Since then, Trump and Huang have appeared together in public repeatedly, and they regularly talk by phone, according to Stephen Witt, the author of The Thinking Machine: Jensen Huang, Nvidia, And The World’s Most Coveted Microchip .
In an interview discussing Huang’s influence over Trump, Witt told NPR that Trump’s recent claims—suggesting that it’s a “hoax” that AI might destroy humanity and that instead AI will be an economic boon—are “exactly Jensen’s talking points.”
“Jensen is now the president’s most influential adviser on technology issues,” Witt said. “The two have become quite close.”
Witt spent time with “tons” of people in the AI industry who share Huang’s views, he told NPR. And like Huang, they tended to downplay risks that software developers—including Nvidia’s biggest customers like Anthropic and OpenAI —are right now urging the White House to take seriously, he found.
“Most of the hardware people, most of the people who designed the networking equipment and the microchips, feel like Jensen does,” Witt said. “They tend to have a very low sense of risk regarding this technology. They just don’t see it.”
He said this debate has been going on between the two camps for the past 10 years and “neither camp has moved at all.” With Huang growing closer to Trump, it seems likely the president will continue downplaying leading AI firms’ warnings and avoiding serious talks with China about their models’ risks. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent confirmed ahead of Trump’s talks with Xi that “the president is completely aligned with Jensen Huang, the CEO of Nvidia.”
According to The Information, China lifting export curbs on Nvidia’s gaming chips “would give Nvidia perhaps its best chance in more than a year to regain some momentum in China’s AI market.” If China gives the nod, ByteDance plans to order 1 million chips, which would automatically secure for Nvidia two quarters of projected sales.
That would certainly help improve Nvidia’s financial outlook in China, as China’s delayed approval of H200 sales meant sales were dismal, comprising less than 1 percent of Nvidia’s data center revenue in the most recent quarter.
Andrew Yoon, a researcher at an AI safety nonprofit called CivAI, told CNBC that in the AI industry, “Nvidia is the most aggressive in terms of, let’s just make money.”
“At every turn, they are really trying to just make sure whatever happens is good for Nvidia’s bottom line,” Yoon said.
If the US and China continue to loosen controls, some experts fear that too many chips may end up being diverted to China. Eventually, that could cause US data centers to lose a precious domestic chip supply that’s currently making it possible to stay ahead on frontier AI, the thinking goes.
Nvidia’s reporting suggests that as of now, the countries don’t compete for resources, though. In the first half of 2026, Nvidia reportedly took a $400 million hit due to vast quantities of unsold H200 chips. No American firms want those chips, since they can access Nvidia’s more advanced chips.
However, demand for chips made for China’s market could perhaps change, as more US data centers come online, policy experts believe .
Nvidia’s spokesperson told Ars that China lifting curbs on “outdated” gaming chips “released nearly a half a decade ago” will only benefit US firms unfairly burdened by restrictions on chips that cannot be used to train AI. The statement recalls Huang’s remarks at a recent “All-In” summit hosted by Trump’s former AI czar David Sacks. Huang publicly promised Trump that “we’re going to make sure that everybody wins in the AI race of America. Every industry, every company, every state, every people.”
Yet, Witt joked that “Jensen is really the only one who wants to sell his equipment to China.”
Witt thinks that a responsible US president would set up a group like the National Transportation Safety Board to review mandatory reports of AI safety incidents. That could support the US-China safety alert system announced last week, which right now troublingly includes no tech experts. But that likely won’t happen since “Jensen has convinced Trump that what’s good for Nvidia is good for America,” Witt said.
It remains unclear if China will approve the gaming chip sales, but sources told The Information that the government intends to allow at least some into the country. The pressure may be on to approve them since “Chinese companies are rolling out AI products and services faster than they can ﬁnd the chips to run them,” The Information noted. At least one buyer “plans to put eight RTX Pro 5500s in each server, a standard setup that lets the chips work together on larger AI models,” sources said. Supposedly, Nvidia’s preparing to ship the first orders this December.
If Huang gets his way, Chinese firms will buy millions more of Nvidia’s chips in the coming years, helping the firm maintain global dominance over companies that are locked in on advancing AI.
During the most recent summit between Trump and Xi, Huang joined many US tech leaders at a state dinner, including Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos, Sam Altman, Mark Zuckerberg, and Satya Nadella. Noticeably, China invited none of its tech leaders.

articles.title_orig: Trump administration cannot tie anti-terrorism grants to election security, judge rules
articles.title_zh: Trump administration cannot tie anti-terrorism grants to election security, judge rules
articles.content_orig:
A judge on Monday vacated a Trump administration rule that would withhold 20% of federal counterterrorism funds allocated for states unless states and certain municipalities made certain changes to how they administer elections.
In his ruling , U.S. District Court Judge Amir Ali said the Federal Emergency Management Agency exceeded its legal authority "by conditioning the counterterrorism grant funds on changes to routine election administration."
Ali also said FEMA , a division of the Department of Homeland Security , had not shown how the desired changes to election administration related to stopping terrorism.
Ali's decision in Washington, D.C., came in response to a lawsuit challenging FEMA's new rule, filed in August by counties in Texas and Tennessee, and the city of Columbus, Ohio.
The Brennan Center for Justice at New York University , which represents some of the plaintiffs in the suit against FEMA and DHS, said on Aug. 17 that FEMA's conditions "violate the Constitution, jeopardize public safety, and put election security at risk."
"Over the last two years, courts have largely blocked the administration's repeated attempts to seize congressional and state authority over elections," the Brennan Center said at the time.  "Now, DHS is holding public safety funding hostage in order to coerce states and local governments into adopting some of the very policies that the administration has tried and failed to impose."
The Brennan Center said the funds that stood to be withheld if FEMA's conditions were allowed to remain in place totaled tens of millions of dollars.
A spokesman for the Department of Justice, which represented DHS and FEMA, declined to comment on Ali's ruling.
Abbie Kamin, the County Attorney of Harris County, Texas, said in a statement, "Today's win is the result of cities and counties standing together against blatant federal overreach that jeopardized public safety."
"The court agreed that holding public safety funding hostage to force the president's agenda is dangerous and illegal," said Kamin, whose county was one of the plaintiffs in the case. "Under our laws, states and localities control our elections, and today's ruling reaffirms that."
FEMA issued the rule in June requiring states "and their respective high-risk urban areas" to make certain changes to election administration or face the withholding of 20% of a state's allocation of counterterrorism funds from the federal government, Ali noted.
Urban areas in the U.S. vote overwhelmingly for Democrats.
The changes include submitting a plan for transitioning from electronic voting systems that use bar codes or QR codes to hand-marked paper ballots; conducting, under federally specified guidelines, a post-election manual audit of 5% of the ballots; and ensuring that each election jurisdiction reconciles the number of voters who voted in a federal election to the number of ballots cast.
The required changes also include verifying the U.S. citizenship of all voters in the state's registration database, and the citizenship of poll workers, election administrators and election-system vendors.
Ali, in his ruling, said, "FEMA's conditions here — which are imposed on states and localities at their own expense, rather than funded by grants, and which address routine election administration decisions rather than the types of terrorist act threats contemplated by the statute — go beyond what Congress authorized."
"For example, the defendants say the ... condition requiring states to adopt FEMA's proposed citizenship-verification procedures in maintaining lists of registered voters 'ensures that only U.S. citizens are voting in U.S. elections,'" Ali wrote.
"But it never explains how that condition, or any of the others, is tied to the goal of shoring up vulnerabilities to terrorist attacks," the judge said.

WASHINGTON — Conservative Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito will no longer participate in a major climate change case after facing calls that he recuse himself because of his stock holdings in oil companies.
The new development was disclosed in a letter dated Monday and sent to lawyers involved in the case, with no reason given.
“Justice Alito has determined that he will not continue to participate in this case,” the letter said.
Alito had, via a court spokeswoman, previously told NBC News there was no need for him to step aside from the case, which is being argued next week and could have broad nationwide implications when the court issues a ruling.
Left-leaning groups have repeatedly called for Alito’s recusal from the case, in which ExxonMobil and Suncor Energy are seeking to toss out a Colorado lawsuit seeking damages from the oil companies for the impacts of climate change.
Although Alito does not own stocks in either company, he does hold stocks in oil companies ConocoPhillips and Phillips 66, as well as five other firms involved in the energy sector, his financial disclosure report says.
Activists calling for his recusal said the companies he holds stocks in could benefit if the Supreme Court throws out the Colorado case, brought by the city and county of Boulder, because it could directly affect similar cases across the country in which they are among the defendants.
The court has a 6-3 conservative majority. With Alito stepping aside, it raises the possibility of a 4-4 split, which would leave the major legal issues unresolved.
The oil and gas industry is hoping the court will issue a broad ruling that would prevent cases like the one in Colorado from moving forward in state courts, potentially saving it from paying out billions of dollars in damages.
Earlier in the litigation, in 2023, Alito did recuse himself when the court turned away an appeal from the companies in the Colorado case.
On the same day, the court rejected appeals in similar cases involving other companies, including ConocoPhillips and Phillips 66. Alito also did not participate in those cases.
In May, a court spokesman said Alito had “inadvertently recused” in the earlier Colorado case.
“Justice Alito does not have a financial interest in any party” involved in the case, the court spokeswoman said in a statement provided to NBC News at the time. Alito was advised by the court’s legal counsel that “his recusal is not required,” she added.
That was before the most recent calls for Alito to step aside based on the indirect benefit he could obtain from a ruling in favor of Exxon and Suncor.
Earlier this month, an advocacy group called Consumer Watchdog pointed to disclosures made by ConocoPhillips and Phillips 66 to shareholders in which they warned of the risks the companies face as a result of climate lawsuits making similar claims to the Colorado case.
“Justice Alito’s recusal ... is the right decision, and one he should have made from the start,” Alexandra Nagy, the group’s organizing director, said in a statement.
The Supreme Court spokeswoman did not immediately respond to a request seeking further comment.
Some conservatives have also pushed for liberal Justice Elena Kagan to recuse herself in the case because of a controversy over a chapter on climate change included in, and subsequently removed from , a reference manual for judges. Kagan wrote a brief foreword to the manual and recently told lawmakers that she never read the chapter in question.
Lawrence Hurley is a senior Supreme Court reporter for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: Ahead of rare execution, lone woman on Tennessee death row says ‘I am at peace’
articles.title_zh: Ahead of rare execution, lone woman on Tennessee death row says ‘I am at peace’
articles.content_orig:
With her execution days away, the lone woman on Tennessee’s death row says she is prepared to die but “nervous” about how the state intends to carry it out.
Before learning Monday that Gov. Bill Lee would not be intervening in her case, Christa Pike wrote in a letter to NBC News, shared by her spiritual adviser: “Whether my clemency is granted or not, I am at peace.”
“I am not afraid to die,” wrote Pike, who has been on death row for over three decades. “I’m only nervous about the process.”
Tennessee is poised to execute Pike, 50, on Wednesday by lethal injection — the first time in more than 200 years that the state will put a woman to death, according to historical records .
In 1995, Pike was 18 when Knoxville police say she and two teenage accomplices tortured, slashed and fatally beat Colleen Slemmer, 19. Police say Pike and the others lured Slemmer, a classmate in their Job Corps training program, to an abandoned steam plant at the nearby University of Tennessee and attacked her.
The case became sensationalized when investigators said it was tied to the occult because someone had carved a pentagram into Slemmer’s chest and Pike bragged to another student that she had kept a fragment of the victim’s skull as a “souvenir.”
Pike doesn’t dispute her role in the grisly killing. But details about her upbringing, marked by years of sexual and physical abuse and neglect, were not shared with the jury that sentenced her to death. Her lawyers believe that if such evidence of abuse were presented at a trial now, a death sentence would not be guaranteed.
They have asked the Supreme Court to halt Pike’s execution, saying that she suffers from post-traumatic stress disorder stemming from being molested and raped beginning when she was a toddler. Being held down and strapped to a gurney, they wrote, will likely create “severe mental suffering and superadded psychological terror under Tennessee’s lethal injection protocol.”
The state hasn’t denied that Pike has suffered from abuse. But in a response filed Monday, the attorney general’s office said a judge already concluded last month that it was “speculative whether Pike would suffer” greater mental harm from how the lethal injection protocol is carried out.
The Supreme Court is Pike’s remaining chance for a reprieve after Lee said he was upholding her death sentence “after deliberate consideration.”
Pike’s lawyers said Monday they were “saddened and heartbroken.”
Another woman, Gaile Owens , was on Tennessee’s death row with Pike until 2010, when Gov. Phil Bredesen changed her sentence to life in prison.
In her letter, Pike wrote that people have seen a “limited public persona that has been the only narrative” about her. Her lawyers had tried to convince Lee that she was a product of a tumultuous childhood.
“Stepping into the chaos of Christa’s life that led her to that moment will not justify her actions that night,” one of her lawyers, Randall Spivey, said of when she committed her crime. “But the chaos will show you that Christa was broken, not evil.”
Pike’s lawyers also point to her age and how it led to such a different outcome in her case.
While she faced a death sentence because of her first-degree murder and conspiracy to commit murder conviction in Slemmer’s death, another conspirator was spared: Pike’s boyfriend, who was 17 at the time. Tadaryl Shipp received a life sentence because he was a juvenile and remains eligible for parole. Shipp testified at his post-conviction hearing that he was the one who carved a pentagram into Slemmer’s chest.
The third accomplice — Shadolla Peterson, then 18 — served as a lookout in the crime and received probation in exchange for her cooperation.
Pike told police she “wasn’t even thinking” when she assaulted Slemmer and that she had been jealous believing the victim was trying to steal Shipp’s attention. Pike’s lawyers say that her age would have been more of a factor today, given how scientific research has evolved in understanding that young people’s brains are still developing well beyond their teen years.
In addition, her lawyers say that her legal representatives at the time could have accepted a deal from prosecutors who were offering a life sentence without parole in return for a guilty plea.
Pike sobbed as the judge told her she would die by electrocution, then the only form of execution in Tennessee before the state moved to lethal injection as its primary method.
She pleaded through tears : “Can I please hug my mom?”
Pike entered prison, where she was placed into solitary confinement for up to 23 hours a day and prescribed Prozac to treat her obsessive-compulsive disorder. Early on, she struggled to express remorse.
“It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I’d done,” Pike said in her clemency petition.
Three years ago, Bethany Brand, a psychologist specializing in trauma, was asked by Pike’s lawyers to assess whether she suffers from psychological disorders and consider if any contributed to the crime.
She sat with Pike at her Nashville prison and reviewed police reports, past medical examinations and other files in her case detailing physical and sexual abuse. Brand learned that Pike’s parents were not stable figures in her life. Her mother’s boyfriends and other men had molested her from a young age, the files said. She did poorly in school, living with other family members in West Virginia and North Carolina. At 17 — one year before she would take part in Slemmer’s murder — Pike reported to North Carolina police that she was walking to the store when a man threw her to the ground and raped her. No one was ever arrested.
In her final report, Brand wrote that the adults in Pike’s life failed her. Doctors only diagnosed a bipolar disorder a few years after she was already in prison.
The level of trauma Pike was subjected to “is almost impossible to grasp because it is so severe,” Brand wrote.
She told NBC News that medications in prison have helped Pike tremendously and that she now has “empathy and great regret” for what she did. But, she added, Pike’s case is a lesson of the need for greater awareness surrounding women’s mental health and recognizing trauma and untreated mental illness.
“In Christa’s case, nobody was trying to get her help,” Brand said.
May Martinez is unconvinced that the person responsible for mutilating her daughter’s body and leaving her nude from the waist up could change.
Martinez recalled how, after the investigation ended, she did not realize all of her daughter’s body parts weren’t buried with her remains, as some had been retained as trial evidence. She had to pick up Slemmer’s skull from the courthouse, and remembers that the medical examiner’s office mailed her other parts later. (The office said it rarely retains human remains as it had 30 years ago because of better technology, enhanced photography and lab work.)
“We had her buried in a Catholic cemetery,” Martinez said. “And she had to be dug up every time they mailed me body parts.”
Recently, she said, she has refused to communicate with Pike directly. The only way she can get justice now is when she watches Pike be executed.
“I will sit there with her picture in my hand,” Martinez said of her daughter, “and as she gets hooked up to a needle to go to sleep, she can look at the picture.”

An all-female execution team may also be assigned.

Congrats are in order for Barbara Palvin and Dylan Sprouse!
The Victoria’s Secret Angel gave birth to her and the actor’s first child together, a baby girl, on Sept. 7, she announced via Instagram on Monday.
“We took Labor Day literally this year,” Palvin, 32, wrote, alongside a photo of herself, Sprouse, 34, and their newborn wearing Los Angeles Dodgers jerseys.
The couple announced in May that they were starting a family , with the model debuting her bump on the Cannes Film Festival red carpet .
Palvin and the former Disney Channel star shared their little one’s gender two months later during the debut episode of the latter’s “Wildmen” podcast with pal Brendan Columbus.
“We are having a baby girl, which I’m very excited about,” Sprouse gushed in July. “I’m excited to be a girl dad, actually … I just unironically love a tea party.”
His wife predicted having a daughter would “mellow” out the “Suite Life of Zack and Cody” alum as he would be only “stressed out” about parenting.
Start your day with Page Six Daily.
Palvin noted that they were “back and forth” on names but had been calling their child “principessa,” which is Italian for princess, while awaiting her arrival.
She continued documenting her pregnancy progress via Instagram, from car selfies to Fourth of July party pics .
Palvin and Sprouse have been together since 2018 — but met the year prior at a party .
The “Suite Life on Deck” alum proposed in September 2022 , waiting until the following summer to share the news.
The couple walked down the aisle in July 2023 in the bride’s native Hungary.
The year before announcing her pregnancy, Palvin went public with her endometriosis struggles — and shared more in a May “L’Beauté” cover story .
“It made me more aware and more patient with myself,” she told the magazine. “I’ve learned that you can’t ignore what your body is telling you; if something feels wrong, don’t ignore it.”
Palvin added, “It changed the way I take care of myself and made me prioritize my health much more seriously.”
Elsewhere in the interview, she praised the “calm and sense of humor” her partner has brought to her life.
“We understand each other’s worlds, but we also keep things super normal at home, which I think is important,” she explained in May. “
“The best part is having someone who’s truly supportive, but also keeps you grounded,” Palvin continued at the time. “We balance each other out.”

articles.title_orig: What Nvidia's $150 billion stock buyback means for shareholders and potential investors
articles.title_zh: What Nvidia's $150 billion stock buyback means for shareholders and potential investors
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia said Monday it has authorized an additional $150 billion to its share buyback program, taking its total to $235 billion, amid record spending on artificial intelligence.
The chip giant said it marks the largest share repurchase authorization increase in history. It expects to complete the total remaining buyback program through fiscal 2028.
Nvidia produces the most advanced chips used for AI and has been a huge beneficiary of the boom in spending on the infrastructure needed to power the tech.
Nvidia's shares have climbed 24% over the past 12 months, lifting the company's market cap to $5.42 trillion. The stock was up 2.8% on Monday.
"NVIDIA's growth is being driven by a once-in-a-generation platform shift to AI and accelerated computing," CEO Jensen Huang said in a statement.
"Our cash generation gives us the capacity to invest in the technologies that advance this transformation and return capital to shareholders," he added. "This authorization reflects our confidence in the long-term opportunity ahead."
Combined hyperscaler capital expenditure is projected to exceed $1.3 trillion by 2027, S&P Global Ratings said in August, as companies race to build AI infrastructure including data centers.
Huang earlier this month said Nvidia would double the number of chips it sells in 2027.
Alongside making the leading chips for AI — graphics processing units — including its Grace Blackwell and Vera Rubin systems, the company produces a variety of additional semiconductors. That includes central processors, or CPUs, switch chips, chips for optical networking, chips for laptops, Jetson chips for robots and cars, and the chip inside Nintendo's Switch 2 gaming console.
"I think we're going through the largest infrastructure build-out in human history, and we have the benefit of being a very central part of that," Huang told CNBC's " Squawk Box " on Monday.
"We're going to generate a lot of cash in the coming years, and every single year, as we generate more cash, we'd like to be able to return it back to shareholders," he said.

articles.title_orig: US FAA delays Boeing 737 MAX 10 certification, shares dive 7%
articles.title_zh: US FAA delays Boeing 737 MAX 10 certification, shares dive 7%
articles.content_orig:
The head of the Federal Aviation Administration said a software problem will delay its certification of the Boeing 737 Max 10 as the agency assesses whether it poses a safety issue, a potential setback for the manufacturer as it seeks to complete government approval of its best-selling family of aircraft.
Boeing had expected to receive a green light from its regulator on the years-delayed planes "very soon," CEO Kelly Ortberg told investors earlier this month. But Boeing said Saturday that last month it flagged a software glitch on some 737 Max aircraft that could affect certain landing procedures.
"We haven't concluded whether this is a safety-of-flight issue or not, but we will be delaying the 10 ... until we're satisfied that we don't have an issue here," FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said at a press conference on air traffic modernization in Washington, D.C., on Monday.
The FAA said in a statement that "safety dictates the certification timeline." It added that the agency was  "following our safety review process to investigate this software glitch and won't hesitate to take action if needed."
Boeing shares extended earlier losses after Bedford's comments, shedding nearly 7% Monday, as investors assessed another delay after years of setbacks for the aircraft.
"We continue to follow the lead of the FAA as we work through the certification process," Boeing said in a statement.
Boeing said over the weekend that the issue could occur with a vertical navigation system after an aircraft misses an approach and has to go around and line up to land again, such as in situations when there is an obstruction on the runway, for example. Both the company and Bedford said pilots are trained for those circumstances.
"The pilots remain in control of the airliner, train for these scenarios," Bedford said Monday. "The issue that we're looking at right now is the workload component."
The FAA certified the Max 7 , the smallest of the family, last month. Those planes have the most updated version of the software, which the FAA is evaluating. It isn't clear how that could affect deliveries of those planes to customers like Southwest Airlines .
U.S. airlines said they don't have any Max aircraft with the issue, in part because they are allowed to revert to older software on those models, if needed, not the newer version that has the potential issue.
Bedford said Boeing had fixed a previous bug in the system but "unexpectedly ... introduced a new bug."
Boeing has been trying to move on from years of safety crises, including two crashes of the Max 8 in 2018  and 2019. A flight control system was implicated in those crashes.
Bedford added on Monday that unlike that system, this "doesn't take control away from the pilots."
The company had originally planned to start delivering the Max 10 in 2020 before those safety concerns and other problems delayed the plane. It is the last of the Max family waiting to be certified.

U.S. Treasury yields edged higher on Monday as pressure on global government bonds resumed, amid higher oil prices and inflation fears.
The 10-year U.S. Treasury note yield —the key benchmark for mortgage borrowing, auto loans and credit card debt — was up more than 5 basis points at 5.234%.
The longer-dated 30-year Treasury bond yield, which is more sensitive to geopolitical risks, was 5 basis points higher at 5.552%.
The 2-year Treasury note yield, which tends to react in line with short-term Federal Reserve interest rate decisions, moved up by more than 6 basis points to 4.926%.
One basis point is equal to 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions.
Bond yields elsewhere also moved higher as anxiety surrounding global government debt and sticky inflation continue to weigh on investors.
The moves follow a volatile week for Treasurys. The benchmark 10-year note yield on Thursday reached its highest rate since June 2007 before easing, while the yield on the 30-year Treasury bond touched levels not seen since 2004.
As global oil prices remained elevated on Monday — with West Texas Intermediate futures trading around $92 a barrel — investors are looking ahead to a flurry of fresh domestic economic data releases this week.
The latest monthly nonfarm payrolls data and unemployment rate are due out later in the week, following the core PCE index and latest quarterly GDP growth print. Before that, August's JOLTS report, expected Tuesday, is forecast to show job openings dipped slightly to 7.24 million month-over-month from 7.27 million in July.

articles.title_orig: GOP Leader Thune Says Taxpayers Shouldn’t Pay for Trump TV Ads
articles.title_zh: GOP Leader Thune Says Taxpayers Shouldn’t Pay for Trump TV Ads
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump has personally driven the controversial, taxpayer-funded video ads promoting himself and his administration’s policies, including helping select the imagery and videos used, a source familiar with the matter told CNN.
Two Trump advisers familiar with the ads said that they were being created in-house by the White House video team — which is part of the communications team, responsible for the administration’s public messaging.
Coming just over a month before the November midterms, the ads have generated bipartisan criticism over how the Trump administration is spending taxpayer dollars.
“It’s a great message. I like the message, but it shouldn’t be paid for with taxpayer dollars,” Senate Majority Leader John Thune told reporters in the Capitol on Monday.
GOP Sen. John Cornyn of Texas echoed that sentiment: “It’s not even a close question.”
The White House has broadly defended the ads, saying they are akin to public service announcements past administrations have put out about Medicare, Obamacare and Covid-19 vaccinations. Officials have insisted they “are very clearly not campaign ads.”
“These public service announcements are about reminding Americans to love their country and understand what makes it worth defending, at home, at our borders, and abroad,” a White House spokesperson said Monday.
But the imagery is undeniably meant to promote Trump, casting him as a warrior battling against existential threats. And the latest one appears nearly identical to a video Trump posted on Truth Social in January 2024, during his third presidential campaign.
That most recent ad shows Trump walking down a hall as audio plays of him saying “this is the final battle.”
“We will cast out the communists, Marxists and fascists. We will throw off the sick political class that hates our country. We will rout the fake news media, and we will liberate America from these villains once and for all,” Trump says in the ad , echoing comments he made during a Veterans Day speech in 2023.
The version on Truth Social has an additional six seconds that includes Trump’s campaign logo and a number to text. The text “Paid for by the US Government” is seen across the screen at the end of the new version of the ad.
Multiple members of Trump’s political operation said they were unaware that these ads were coming until they aired. But another source pushed back on the notion that anyone was kept in the dark — noting that the president had spoken about the ads to multiple aides and advisers and insisting that they were not being made in secret.
The latest ad — which aired during at least two NFL games on Sunday, during Fox’s broadcasts of the Washington Commanders-Seattle Seahawks matchup as well as the Carolina Panthers-Cleveland Browns game — is the third government-funded message in recent days to be captured by the media tracker AdImpact.
An ad that began airing Wednesday featured rapidly edited pictures and video of Trump over audio of him denouncing communism and socialism. Text on the screen touted his administration’s accomplishments, including “reigniting American manufacturing.”
“The ad is educational and unapologetically patriotic,” a White House spokesperson said in a statement. “We should be proud of our country.”
A second ad features video of Trump at Mount Rushmore as his voice is heard saying, “Never before has any nation celebrated so magnificent a triumph as this one.”
Democratic Rep. Jamie Raskin, the ranking member of the House Judiciary Committee, said in a post on X that the ads “may be felony criminal theft and conversion of government property for political campaign purposes.”
And Raskin, who will gain congressional subpoena power in November if Democrats win the House, said it is not just Trump who might face inquiries over the messages. He said the creation of the ads was a “Hatch Act violation for any government employees who worked on it or used government resources to make it.”
“This is dumb, dumb, dumb beyond belief,” one former Trump campaign official told CNN. “These guys are all gonna get subpoenaed. It’s gonna be bad.”

articles.title_orig: Foie gras, live dolphins and toasters: China and US cut reciprocal tariffs on $30bn each of goods
articles.title_zh: Foie gras, live dolphins and toasters: China and US cut reciprocal tariffs on $30bn each of goods
articles.content_orig:
World’s biggest economies release lists of products in latest move away from trade war – but no strategic goods are included
The US and China have released reciprocal lists of goods worth about $30bn each on which they plan to cut tariffs, ranging from consumer electronics and agricultural products to artificial flowers and live dolphins.
The announcements are the latest tack away from the intense trade war between the world’s two largest economies that dominated much of last year, though major strategic products are not included and no timeline has yet been given for the reductions.
The US list includes 77 categories of Chinese products including bed linen, garden umbrellas, toasters, fish hooks and billiard balls. The reciprocal Chinese list features 1,619 types of US product including a broad range of food such as butter, offal, lobster and foie gras.
It also includes coal, scientific devices such as MRI systems, rabbit hair and several types of animals for breeding.
Han Lin, the China country director at The Asia Group, a strategic advisory firm, said: “The animal list is certainly eye-catching: donkeys, mules, horses, whales, dolphins and dugongs. But I’d read it less as an exotic trade story than as evidence of how granular tariff codes can be.”
The news comes days after Xi Jinping and Donald Trump met in Washington for an optics-driven summit aimed at stabilising the two sides’ volatile relationship.
Zhu Tian, a vice-president and co-dean at the China Europe International Business School (CEIBS) in Shanghai, said: “It is a positive step, but not a major breakthrough.” He noted that the reductions covered a relatively small share of US-China trade, and that other tariffs on more strategic goods remained in place.
“Still, it is significant that the two sides are moving from simply avoiding further escalation to actually reducing some tariffs,” he added.
The agreement has been brokered through the US-China Board of Trade, set up during Trump’s visit to Beijing in May .
The US trade representative Jamieson Greer said each side had recommended $30bn of non-sensitive trade that “could benefit from more favourable tariff treatment in the future”. The list represented “improved market access for about 30% of US exports to China”, he added.
The Chinese commerce ministry said levies on more than 90% of the products would be subject to “most favoured nation” levels, according to state media.
Sensitive product categories such as semiconductors, batteries and electric vehicles are not covered in the $30bn tariff cut lists.
US whole soya beans imports – which became a Chinese target during 2025’s trade war – are not on Beijing’s tally, Reuters news agency noted, meaning they still face an additional tariff of 10%.
Meanwhile, the Xi-Trump meeting last week yielded only a two-month extension to a wider trade truce first established by the two leaders in Busan , South Korea, last year.
Lin said: “Both sides are carving out non-sensitive trade where cooperation is still possible. It’s managed stabilisation, not a trade reset.”

articles.title_orig: Benjamin Satterley, globetrotting wrestler known as Pac, dies at 40
articles.title_zh: Benjamin Satterley, globetrotting wrestler known as Pac, dies at 40
articles.content_orig:
Benjamin Satterley, the hard-hitting and high-flying professional wrestler known to fans worldwide simply as Pac, has died, All Elite Wrestling announced Sunday night. He was 40.
News of his death came the day after he’d wrestled during AEW’s “All Out” pay-per-view Saturday night at the NOW Arena in Hoffman Estates, Illinois, outside Chicago. A cause of death was not immediately provided.
In a statement Monday, the police department in Des Plaines, Illinois, said there were no immediate indications of foul play and that the circumstances surrounding Satterley’s death were not considered suspicious.
“A native of Newcastle upon Tyne, England, Satterley began his wrestling career in 2004 and went on to perform for wrestling organizations all over the world, captivating fans with innovative high-flying moves and incredible in-ring ability,” AEW said.
Satterley first began training at 18 and made a name for himself on the British independent scene before embarking on a globetrotting career in which he performed in some of the biggest promotions on the planet, including AEW, World Wrestling Entertainment (where he went by Adrian Neville), New Japan Pro-Wrestling and Consejo Mundial de Lucha Libre.
But it wasn’t until he saw the crowd reaction to one of his matches at a much smaller venue — Southern California indie promotion Pro Wrestling Guerrilla — that he finally thought he could make a career of professional wrestling.
At the time, he was still working night shifts at a courier factory, he told Colt Cabana in the “Art of Wrestling” podcast .
“I look back on it very fondly, but it was a tough time in my life,” he said.
Satterley arrived in WWE in 2012 to much fanfare. During his roughly six-year run with the company, he became the NXT Champion, NXT Tag Team Champion and WWE Cruiserweight Champion.
His high-flying offense, made all the more impressive by the brawny physique on his stocky frame, earned him the nickname “The Man That Gravity Forgot.”
That physique played a direct role in choosing Pac as his ring name. In an interview with Chris Jericho on the “Talk Is Jericho” podcast, he recalled having six-pack abs even as a kid. He would play fight with his dad, Satterley said, and his father would tell him to show him his abs, which eventually translated into a “silly nickname.”
When he started training and had to choose a name, Satterley couldn’t think of anything else. “It was only meant to be kind of a temporary thing, but then it kind of — it’s one of those names that kind of, it just stuck,” he said.
Satterley debuted on All Elite Wrestling in 2019, where he’d eventually earn the moniker “The Bastard.”
In AEW, he won the All-Atlantic Championship in 2022 and became one of the company’s more prominent wrestlers as part of the Death Riders faction, with whom he’d earn the AEW World Trios Championship alongside fellow members Claudio Castagnoli and Wheeler Yuta in 2025. It followed another Trios title in 2022 alongside Penta El Zero Miedo and Rey Fénix as part of the “Death Triangle.”
Between the ropes, few wrestlers could combine speed, agility, technique and raw power quite like Satterley.
He could twist and wind his body off the top turnbuckle with his signature “Black Arrow,” or he could use his “Brutalizer” to tie up an opponent’s arms and neck on the canvas.
On the microphone, his promos conveyed no-nonsense intensity that relayed an ultimately simple message to opponents: I’m here to hurt you.
“My name is ‘The Bastard,’” Satterley said in one AEW promo. “The people named me that because I am a bastard. But on top of that — in addition to — I just so happen to be an excellent, exceptional, world-class professional wrestler.”
But that bravado belied a much shier quality outside the ring.
“I’ve got this kind of rejection complex, you know,” he told Cabana. “I fear failure, that’s kind of my thing. That’s kind of what holds me back in a lot of aspects of my life, especially professionally.”
Satterley grappled with his insecurities on the podcast but concluded that insecurities are part of human nature and that sharing them with the world could ultimately be a force for good.
“Maybe people can relate to the human side of me, rather than just whatever I do in the ring,” he said.
Tributes to Satterley quickly followed news of his death.
“The greatest export from our country,” fellow Englishman and AEW World Champion Will Ospreay said on X . “Also the greatest human being.”
“I am in shock. This is heartbreaking,” AEW wrestler Evil Uno said . “We have lost another great person, a great soul, a true professional.”
Ace Austin, whom Satterley defeated on a special episode of AEW’s “Collision” program Wednesday, summed up what many were feeling Sunday: “I don’t understand man.”
AEW referee Bryce Remsburg remarked on a decadeslong friendship with Satterley.
“To many, he was a bastard,” Remsburg said on X . “To my kids, he was Ben — who brought them Kinder Eggs from the UK, who converted them to Newcastle fans. To me, he was an incredible friend for 20 years.”
Speaking to fans during an indie show Sunday night, fellow Death Riders stablemate Marina Shafir said Satterley “was our bastard.”
“I was just holding this man yesterday,” she said, her voice breaking.
She recalled talking with Satterley about “wiener dogs” and basketball courts.
“He was just so modest about how fascinating he was. ... I wouldn’t be here today if I didn’t share time and space with this man,” Shafir said.
Rudy Chinchilla is a breaking news editor for NBC News Digital.

UNITED NATIONS - Slovenian Prime Minister Janez Janša accused the United Nations of applying double standards to global conflicts, arguing that the international community's focus on Gaza has overshadowed Russia's war in Ukraine and other humanitarian crises, while revealing that President Donald Trump has promised to visit Slovenia, the homeland of first lady Melania Trump .
Speaking exclusively to Fox News Digital on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York on Wednesday, Janša said the international body must give greater attention to conflicts beyond the Middle East rather than concentrating its diplomatic efforts on a single crisis.
"We have to get rid of double standards," Janša said, calling for the U.N. to apply its available diplomatic and security tools equally instead of putting its attention, money and energy into one conflict while neglecting others.
MIDDLE EAST TAKES CENTER STAGE AT UN AS REGIONAL LEADERS CONFRONT IRAN WAR, GAZA AND HOUTHI THREAT
Right-wing Slovenian Democratic Party (SDS) leader Janez Janša addresses the media after his investiture vote as Slovenia's Prime Minister at the National Assembly in Ljubljana on May 22, 2026. (Jure Makovec / AFP via Getty Images)
The Slovenian leader said he was struck by how extensively Gaza dominated speeches during the opening of the General Assembly , while Ukraine, a war much closer to his country's borders, received comparatively less attention.
For Slovenia and other European countries, he said, Russia's invasion represents an immediate security threat, with no clear indication that Moscow is prepared to negotiate an end to the fighting.
Janša argued that the U.N. was established to prevent such conflicts and should not allow its attention to be consumed by one region.
He also pointed to the persecution of Christians in Nigeria and other humanitarian crises, arguing that the international body must recognize that different countries face different security and humanitarian challenges.
TRUMP TO ZERO-IN ON IRAN NUCLEAR THREAT, GAZA PLAN AND UN OVERHAUL IN WORLD STAGE SPEECH
An office building burns following a Russian drone attack in central Odesa, Ukraine, on Friday, Sept. 18, 2026. (Michael Shtekel/AP)
Janša said he intends to raise the issue during his own address to the General Assembly, scheduled for Thursday.
His criticism comes as Slovenia undergoes a significant shift in its foreign policy, particularly toward Israel.
Under the previous government of Prime Minister Robert Golob, Slovenia recognized Palestinian statehood in June 2024 and imposed an arms embargo on Israel in July 2025. The government defended those measures as necessary to protect Palestinian civilians and uphold international law.
Since returning to power, Janša has sought to strengthen Slovenia's relationship with Israel, marking a shift from the previous government's more critical approach toward the Jewish state.
Earlier this month, Israel opened its first resident embassy in Slovenia, while Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar visited the country for talks aimed at expanding political and economic cooperation. The two governments also signed a cooperation program covering education, science, culture, youth and sports through 2030.
Janša described his government's approach as a return to the traditionally good relations between the two countries rather than a dramatic diplomatic realignment.
US-BACKED ISRAEL-MOROCCO DEAL DEEPENS ABRAHAM ACCORDS AMID GROWING REGIONAL THREATS
President Donald Trump and Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy shake hands as they meet on the sidelines of the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York City in this handout released September 22, 2026. (Ukrainian Presidential Press Service/Handout via Reuters)
He also criticized European governments that, in his view, have failed to recognize the broader strategic connections between Iran , Russia and the conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East.
Janša said he has supported the Iranian opposition for decades and argued that lasting peace in the Middle East would remain elusive without political change in Tehran.
He accused some European governments of applying inconsistent standards by supporting Ukraine while taking positions toward Iran that he believes fail to account for Tehran’s relationship with Moscow, citing Ireland and Spain as well as Slovenia under the previous government before this year’s change in leadership.
Janša also suggested that some European leaders have used the Palestinian issue to divert public attention from domestic economic and political problems, particularly ahead of elections.
The prime minister's visit to New York also provided an opportunity to strengthen Slovenia's relationship with Washington, a relationship that carries a personal dimension because of the country's most prominent American connection: First Lady Melania Trump.
Born in Slovenia in 1970, Melania Trump grew up in the town of Sevnica before moving to the United States and becoming the nation's second foreign-born first lady.
The prime minister praised Melania Trump’s work on initiatives for children, describing her role in the White House as a source of pride for many Slovenians. He said his wife met the first lady for the first time on Tuesday and that he also spoke briefly with President Trump.

According to Janša, he invited Trump to visit Slovenia and received a positive response. "He promised he'll come," Janša told Fox News Digital.

articles.content_orig:
The U.S. ambassador to China said Trump offered to sell arms to China.
Trump administration officials said on Monday that the United States has no plans to sell weapons to China after U.S. Ambassador to China David Perdue indicated during a televised interview that President Donald Trump offered a weapons deal to China's Xi Jinping during a high-profile summit last week .
"President Trump continues to say, 'Hey, we sell arms to other people around the world,'" Perdue said Sunday during an appearance on Fox News. "He actually asked President Xi would he like to buy some at one point."
Perdue did not provide further details about the offer, and he did not reveal Xi's response.
A U.S. official denied there were plans to sell weapons to China.
"The U.S. government has no plans to sell weapons to China," the official said to ABC News on Monday.
The State Department also denied a potential sale, saying in a statement to ABC News that "U.S. law prohibits arms sales to China and there is no offer or plan to sell arms to China."
Asked about Perdue's comments in the Oval Office on Monday, Trump said he "didn't discuss it" with Xi, suggesting he meant Taiwan instead of China.
"I never heard of that one. I'm going to have to ask him. You mean we're going to sell? Now they'd probably like to buy it because we do make better equipment than them. So maybe it's a good idea. Yeah, but, we didn't discuss it," Trump said, later adding "I think he probably was talking about Taiwan."
A U.S. weapons sale offer to China would be extraordinary, as China is viewed as the primary strategic and economic competitor of the U.S. and is designated as a foreign adversary. The U.S. has placed extensive economic sanctions on China, including economic restrictions, investment bans and contract limits on companies, groups and schools tied to the Chinese military.
The two geopolitical rivals are also competing in the race to develop advanced artificial intelligence and have opposing views over Taiwanese sovereignty.
And in recent weeks, Beijing has come under scrutiny for allegedly providing another U.S. adversary -- Iran -- with satellite imagery in their ongoing conflict with the U.S. and other regional allies.
Perdue told Fox News that Xi had "assured" Trump during their bilateral meeting last week that they were "looking into" the allegations about supporting Iran with satellite imagery.
The Trump administration notably downplayed taking action against China for allegedly helping Iran despite the United States' stated goal of targeting all countries with financial ties to Iran as part of the U.S. Treasury's offensive "Operation Economic Outcast."
"When they say that China spies on us, I say, 'You’re right, and we spy on them too,' you know? We spy on them too," Trump said earlier this month.
When asked by reporters on Friday if the two leaders had discussed the war in Iran, Trump replied, "We did," adding without providing details: "I think we’re going to do great."
The potential offer to China comes as the Trump administration continues to press pause on a proposed $14 billion arms sale to the island of Taiwan, a de facto independent nation.
China has long claimed the sovereign territory as its own and regularly conducts large-scale military drills, live-fire exercises and daily air and naval patrols to apply pressure on the island. Taiwan relies heavily on U.S. military support to push back on China's encroachments.
Perdue said that the administration was not denying Taiwan access to weapons needed for its defense, asserting: "President Trump is as strong on Taiwan as I've ever seen anybody. He's made it very clear that we have not changed the One China policy."
"President Xi has heard that repeatedly from President Donald Trump. President Trump has already sold 50% more arms to Taiwan than any other president since 1979," Perdue added.
ABC News' Nicholas Kerr contributed to this report.

Following Samsung’s lead , another tech giant appears ready to launch a new widescreen foldable, and this one has some serious history behind it. Apple’s iPhone Duo marks that company’s entry into the foldable market , but Motorola isn’t really entering the market. The company has long made clamshell foldables, and after expanding into the book-style market earlier this year, it may now be planning to enter the widescreen foldable market — and today we’re getting our best preview yet.
We’ve known about Motorola’s widescreen foldable intentions for a while now. Those intentions are now actually starting to take shape with the Razr Wide Fold. We’ve seen leaked sketches and a briefly teased silhouette of the device in the past, and a new set of Android Headlines reports are now giving us a look at the device’s physical mock-ups and specs .
The renders match what we’ve been expecting, while the specs paint a clearer picture of how the upcoming device could stand against the likes of the Z Fold 8, iPhone Duo, and the Xiaomi 18 Fold. From the outside, the upcoming device appears to be very similar to its counterparts mentioned earlier. It’s stubby, with an expansive front screen that opens up into a landscape-oriented display that could be great for consuming content, multitasking, and gaming. The rear features a camera setup that looks similar to what we’ve seen in early sketches.
From the looks of it, the Motorola widescreen foldable will have much rounder edges, similar to the iPhone Duo and unlike the Z Fold 8’s sharp and angular aesthetic. The new foldable will also reportedly be smaller and thicker.
The Z Fold 8 measures in at 9.7mm when folded, while the Razr Wide Fold is expected to measure in at 12.6mm. It’s also expected to feature a smaller 6.92-inch inner display, compared to the Z Fold 8’s 7.6-inch display.
The extra thickness, complete with a smaller overall frame, should result in a relatively similar weight profile to the Z Fold 8 and iPhone Duo. This gives us a pretty good idea of what the upcoming device could feel like in hand, but physical mock-ups only tell us so much. They don’t reveal much about the display itself, or how Motorola might be using that extra bulk. That’s where the accompanying spec leak starts filling in the blanks.
The 6.92-inch inner display will reportedly be an OLED panel with a 1,28 x 2,364 pixel resolution and a 165Hz refresh rate. The cover display would reportedly measure 4.97 inches with a 1,732 x 1,140 pixel resolution. France may have a highly secularized culture, but it has given Pope Leo XIV a superstar welcome.
In Paris, around 800,000 lined the Champs-Élysées avenue, some waving Vatican or French flags while others climbed trees or stood on each other’s shoulders to get a glimpse of the popemobile. In Lourdes, a holy site in southern France, around 150,000 attended an open-air papal Mass, according to Vatican estimates which dwarf the numbers of faithful who turned out for the last papal visit in 2008.
During the four-day visit, Leo appeared comfortable and relaxed, delivering most of his speeches and reflections in French, as the Chicago-born pontiff sought to tackle several themes during the trip.
A strong focus of Leo’s has been on trying to revitalize faith in a traditional European Catholic heartland as well as on addressing the clerical sexual abuse scandal and big political topics such as artificial intelligence. He’s also offered some more personal, unscripted remarks, helping to shape a clearer picture of himself.
While his predecessor never made official visits to the major Catholic European countries of France and Spain, Pope Leo has traveled to both within the first year and a half since his election.
France is sometimes described as the “eldest daughter of the church” because of its deep Catholic roots, but it’s also faced a long-term trend of declining church attendance with estimates of just 5-8% of the population heading to the pews each week.
French bishops have more recently reported some good news though: a surprising rise in new church entrants after around 8,200 adolescents and 13,200 adults were baptized in 2026. That’s a 20% increase on the year prior, with the church also saying 42% of the adults seeking baptism are aged 18-25, a reflection of a trend showing Gen Z’s openness to religious faith .
It’s something Pope Leo will have noted at the Stade de France when 80,000 young people packed the venue for a jubilant – and loud – prayer vigil. It was similar to when the pontiff visited Spain in June.
“There is a quest for meaning. People need and are in search of meaning and answers to the big existential question,” Rev. Benoît Pouzin, a priest in southwest France involved in youth ministry, told CNN.
France has a strict separation between church and state, so each papal visit needs to be carefully navigated. But in a surprising twist, Leo’s Mass in Paris was celebrated on the Place de la Concorde, a site deeply linked to the secular Republic as it’s where the last king of France, Louis XVI and Marie-Antoinette were guillotined. The separation of the church started with the fall of the monarchy during the French Revolution.
In another unusual move later in the trip, President Emmanuel Macron also attended a papal Mass in Metz, a city in the northeast, despite criticism in 2023 for doing the same during Pope Francis’ visit.
Many among the crowds also pointed to Leo’s role as the other major US leader on the world stage. It’s hard not to see him as a counterweight to President Donald Trump. In contrast to the Trump administration, the pope has called for stronger guardrails around the development of artificial intelligence, warning against a “paradise of machines” while in Paris.
Pope Leo said he is taking the warnings about Artificial Intelligence’s threat to humanity seriously, and said it is irresponsible for people to sit back and dismiss the risks of AI.
Trump has dismissed the warnings about AI as a “hoax” which he made during a surprise phone call with Jensen Huang, the CEO of chipmaker Nvidia, at a summit in Los Angeles.
“I don’t think that that is fake news – as some have said – to try and pause,” Leo XIV said on board the papal plane from Metz to Rome.
Leo, who has expressed a keen interest in artificial intelligence since the start of his papacy, said that he found it “interesting” that Huang had unveiled a new tool to prevent AI agents from operating out of human control.
“He’s the same one, however, that says there should be no limits placed and no government regulation,” the Pope said.
The pope devoted his first major theological document to AI earlier this year, warning about the use of AI in warfare and calling for stronger ethical foundation to the development of the technology.
The pope explained that the Vatican had established its own AI commission to understand how to use it, along with the risks and benefits, and that “we need to continue to invite political leaders, the leaders of AI” so they can “look at what is happening already and what could be down the road.”
He explained: “We are trying to continue to promote dialog, study, investigation, to find ways to make sure that AI does not get to a point where it could destroy humanity.”
“If someone were to ask me, am I in panic mode? No, I’m not, I sleep at night” the pope said, but added: “I do think that the concerns raised by many of the experts, specialists in AI, should be taken seriously.”
“To simply say, oh, it’s not going to happen and close our eyes to it, I think, is probably not the most responsible way to go about that,” Leo said.
The pope, who spoke out against the US war in Iran, also wants a more united Europe, a stronger European Union and stronger international cooperation. “Today, relations between individuals and states are becoming increasingly uncivilized,” the pope said in Metz on Monday. “The value of keeping one’s word is dismissed; instead, people boast of lies and deceit.”
The pope’s speech also praised one of the founders of the European Union, Robert Schuman, for whom there is an ongoing formal cause to make a saint.
Pope Leo XIV has warned against the use of Christianity by far-right political groups, while calling on the church to be active in seeking to prevent extremism. Speaking on board the papal plane, he said that “the combination of these far-right points of view with a certain kind of religion” cannot be considered an “authentic expression of Christianity.”
The pope’s comments came in response to a question about the rise of extremist parties in Germany as he flew back from making a major speech on European Unity at the French-German border.
“We go back to the values of the Gospel [Christian teaching], which are not about hatred and division, but they’re about understanding and compassion,” the pope said.
The American pontiff also responded to Trump’s White House media ban, which includes CNN and other outlets. In answer to a question from CNN, he said he was “very happy that, here, you are all welcome and good coverage, I think, is very important and that we have it all the way around, for everyone.” The response was classic Leo: signaling his support for the press but not wishing to create an unnecessary dispute with the president.
The American pope’s in-flight interactions with journalists were rare, unscripted moments, with his answers often revealing more about his personality. On the flight from Rome to Paris, the pope was asked if he had anything to do with a miraculous recent Chicago White Sox victory, his beloved baseball team. “No comment,” he said before adding with a smile, “Great things happen in Chicago.”
He also recalled childhood memories of watching Fulton Sheen, the American archbishop and broadcaster who was recently declared “blessed,” one step ahead of sainthood, and revealed he’d been practicing his French but was no longer using the Duolingo language app. “It’s fake news!” he said about recent reports. Leo has in the past been spotted using Duolingo to learn German.
Leo isn’t simply vocal about challenges of his homeland. He also voiced concern over assisted dying with France recently approving legislation granting the right to the incurably ill, which is strongly opposed by the Catholic Church. Leo spoke on the subject several times during his visit – most clearly in the “miracle shrine” town of Lourdes, known for drawing many sick and terminally ill pilgrims to its shrine.
